title: AI is Oil, Not God
gist: Packy McCormick reads the July 24, 2026 open-weight-model letter signed by Satya Nadella, Jensen Huang and others as a textbook commoditize-your-complement play: every signatory profits when models get cheap and plentiful, which erodes the Anthropic/OpenAI frontier duopoly. He argues the signatories' willingness to push diffusion is revealed evidence that the people closest to the technology see AI as 'Oil, not God', and reprints Matt Kaufman's counter on fine-tuning away bio/cyber safeguards. The post cuts off at a Substack paywall gate before McCormick's full reply to Kaufman is shown.

insights.claim: The July 2026 letter supporting open-weight models, signed by Satya Nadella, Jensen Huang and other tech leaders, is best explained by Joel Spolsky's Strategy Letter V logic that smart companies commoditize their products' complements rather than by any principled stance on openness.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Read corporate AI-policy advocacy as a positioning tell: a firm's stated openness stance maps to where its margin pool sits in the stack.
insights.quote: “Smart companies try to commoditize their products’ complements.” – Joel Spolsky, Strategy Letter V
insights.locator: From a business perspective, this is classic tech strategy stuff.

insights.claim: Every signatory of the open-weight letter either produces open-weight models or sells a complement to them: models run on Nvidia chips, power Microsoft products, live on Hugging Face, and run on machines Dell sells, while a16z and Y Combinator back companies that use and compete with models.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The signatory list is a ready-made basket of businesses whose economics improve as model inference gets commoditized — the picks-and-shovels and application layers, not the labs.
insights.quote: Models run on Nvidia chips. They power Microsoft products.
insights.locator: All of the signatories either make open-weight models

insights.claim: Palantir's Alex Karp has been publicly pushing open-weight models because commoditized models let Palantir disintermediate the model layer inside enterprise deployments.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Enterprise software vendors capture more value the cheaper models get; watch Palantir-style middleware as a beneficiary of open-weight diffusion.
insights.quote: Palantir’s Alex Karp has been banging this drum because he wants to disintermediate models in the enterprise.
insights.locator: All of the signatories either make open-weight models

insights.claim: CrowdStrike's support for open weights follows from a defender-parity argument: security incumbents benefit when defenders have access to the same intelligence attackers do.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Cyber-security vendors are structurally long open models — a direct rebuttal to the 'open weights are a security risk' short thesis on the sector.
insights.quote: CrowdStrike benefits if defenders have access to the same intelligence as attackers.
insights.locator: All of the signatories either make open-weight models

insights.claim: Box, ServiceNow, Replit and Perplexity all improve as capable models become cheaper, more plentiful and easier to customize, which is why they signed the open-weight letter.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Application-layer software with model input costs is the clearest gross-margin beneficiary of falling open-model prices.
insights.locator: Box, ServiceNow, Replit and Perplexity all get better

insights.claim: Google joined the open-weight letter as a new signatory despite institutional slowness because it wins in either regime, and open source models may eventually let it serve search ads more cheaply.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Cheap open models are a cost-of-goods lever on Google's ad-serving stack, not just a competitive threat to its model franchise.
insights.quote: Google, a new signatory, got off of its slow, bureaucratic ass and signed because Google will be fine either way, and maybe open source models will allow it to serve search ads more cheaply at some point.
insights.locator: Google, a new signatory, got off of its slow

insights.claim: Roughly $8 trillion of combined market capitalization came out in support of open-weight models because it serves the signatories' own business interests while also happening to benefit consumers.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The scale of the corporate coalition backing diffusion sets the political baseline against which lock-down regulation must now fight.
insights.quote: $8 trillion worth of market cap coming out in support of open-weight models because it's good for their business and makes them look good...

insights.claim: More competition at the model layer directly reduces the ability of Anthropic and OpenAI to run away with the frontier and build a duopoly, and each additional unit of that competition benefits the letter's signatories.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The open-weight coalition is effectively a coordinated attack on frontier-lab pricing power — a negative for private-market frontier-lab valuations and a positive for model consumers.
insights.quote: The more competition there is at the model layer, the less Anthropic and OpenAI are able to run away with the frontier and build a duopoly, the more each of the signatories benefits.
insights.locator: The more competition there is at the model layer

insights.claim: Corporate advocacy for open weights is a selfish act whose private incentives happen to coincide with the interests of consumers and millions of businesses, which is presented as capitalism working rather than as altruism.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Don't discount the durability of the pro-open coalition on grounds of insincerity — incentive-aligned advocacy is more persistent than values-based advocacy.
insights.quote: Signing this letter is a selfish act that also happens to align with the interests of consumers and millions of businesses.
insights.locator: Signing this letter is a selfish act

insights.claim: The entire open-versus-locked-down AI debate reduces to whether one believes AI is an economically useful commodity that can be scaled and refined as a multiplier on everything we do, or a supremely intelligent being that will wake up and make humanity subservient.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A clean sorting axis for AI-policy risk: commodity-framing implies volume/price-decline economics, deity-framing implies regulatory tail risk on distribution.
insights.quote: more “an economically useful commodity that can be scaled and refined to act as a multiplier on everything we do” or “supremely intelligent and powerful being that’s going to wake up and make humanity subservient (if we're lucky).”
insights.locator: I think it comes down to whether you think AI is more Oil or God

insights.claim: The author has held the commodity view of AI unchanged since writing The Goldilocks Zone in June 2024, indicating a multi-year stable prior rather than a reaction to the latest news cycle.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Signals a stable analytical frame worth tracking for consistency — useful when weighting the author's future AI calls.
insights.quote: I am strongly on the Oil side, as I wrote in The Goldilocks Zone in June 2024. My belief is unchanged since.
insights.locator: I am strongly on the Oil side

insights.claim: The fact that Satya Nadella and Jensen Huang, who sit at the bleeding edge of the technology, publicly backed open-weight diffusion is revealed-preference evidence that they do not privately expect models to become conscious and take over, since no short-term incentive would justify that risk if they did.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A tradeable read on insider AGI belief: the people with the best information are behaving like commodity suppliers, not like custodians of a superintelligence.
insights.quote: Surely, if they saw something that made them believe that these models were going to become conscious and take over the world, they wouldn’t be as openly pro-diffusion, even if they were short-term incentivized to be.
insights.locator: In fact, I think it’s super interesting that Satya and Jensen

insights.claim: Matt Kaufman of Collaborative Fund argues that open-weight proliferation is dangerous because models can be fine-tuned to strip out bio and cyber safeguards, something he calls trivially easy today and likely to matter once open models get much more powerful and once dangerous actors outside the tech bubble catch on.
insights.speaker: Matt Kaufman, Collaborative Fund
insights.so_what: The strongest near-term regulatory attack surface on open weights is fine-tuning-based safeguard removal — watch for rules targeting post-training rather than release itself.
insights.quote: I’d definitely prefer a more open ecosystem were it not for risks like models being fine-tuned to remove bio / cyber safeguards, and then resulting in harm. This seems trivially easy and perhaps isn’t a big issue now
insights.locator: Just saw your tweet on the Jensen note

insights.claim: Because there are many domains in which large language models favor offense over defense, a case exists for regulating them as tightly as weapons.
insights.speaker: Matt Kaufman, Collaborative Fund
insights.so_what: Weapons-style regulation is the tail-risk scenario for the open-weight trade; it would invert the beneficiary list of the commoditize-complements thesis.
insights.quote: I think there are many domains where LLMs more favor offense rather than defense so this feels like a scary reality and I therefore sympathize with arguments that they should be tightly regulated like weapons.
